events.description: Increased API error rates begin for DynamoDB; all systems connecting via the public us-east-1 endpoint experience DNS failures. Global table replication lag to and from us-east-1 is prolonged.
DWFM state checks begin to fail because the process depends on DynamoDB; between 11:48 PM and 2:24 AM, droplet leases slowly time out.
ECS, EKS and Fargate begin experiencing container launch failures and cluster scaling delays.
Redshift query and cluster operations begin failing while DynamoDB endpoints are down.
Lambda begins experiencing function creation/update failures and invocation errors; STS begins experiencing API errors.
AWS Management Console sign-in begins failing for IAM users due to DynamoDB issues.
AWS Support Center begins experiencing issues; it fails over to another region as designed, but an account metadata subsystem returns invalid responses.
Amazon Connect begins experiencing elevated errors handling calls, chats and cases.
Engineers identify DynamoDB's DNS state as the source of the outage.
Temporary mitigations enable some internal services to connect to DynamoDB and repair key internal tooling, unblocking further recovery.
Amazon Connect errors end.
STS API errors recover temporarily.
AWS Management Console sign-in failures end.
ECS, EKS and Fargate container launch failures and cluster scaling delays end.
Redshift query and cluster operations recover for most clusters (some clusters remain impacted until 4:05 AM Oct 21).
All DNS information for DynamoDB is restored; customers begin resolving the endpoint as cached DNS records expire, fully by 2:40 AM.

DWFM begins re-establishing leases across the EC2 fleet; EC2 APIs return 'insufficient capacity' errors and lease work times out, with DWFM unable to make forward progress. EC2 launch impairment begins.
All global table replicas are fully caught up.
DynamoDB increased API error rates end; AWS Support Center failover-related issues end.
Engineers throttle incoming work and begin selective restarts of DWFM hosts, clearing queues and allowing leases to be established.
The Lambda internal subsystem polling SQS queues, which failed and did not recover automatically, is restored.
DWFM has established leases with all droplets in us-east-1; new EC2 launches begin to succeed, though many requests see 'request limit exceeded' errors due to throttling.
Network Manager begins propagating network configurations to newly launched instances, with a significant backlog.
Network Load Balancer (NLB) begins experiencing increased connection errors for some load balancers.
Network Manager latencies increase as it works through the backlog; new instances launch but lack network connectivity. Engineers work to reduce load on Network Manager.

Monitoring detects NLB health check issues caused by new EC2 instances being brought into service before network state propagates; engineers begin remediation. Alternating health check results degrade the health check subsystem, triggering automatic AZ DNS failover.

NLB health check failures trigger Lambda instance terminations, leaving Lambda under-scaled; engineers throttle asynchronous work to prioritize synchronous invocations. Amazon Connect experiences a second period of errors due to NLB and Lambda impact.
STS experiences a second period of API errors due to NLB health check failures.
Engineers disable automatic health check failover for NLB, bringing healthy nodes and targets back into service and resolving connection errors.
STS API errors end.
Network propagation times return to normal; new EC2 launches operate normally. Launches begin to succeed from 10:37 AM, though some newly launched instances have connectivity issues until 1:50 PM.
Engineers begin relaxing request throttles.
All EC2 APIs and new instance launches operate normally.
Automatic DNS health check failover for NLB is re-enabled after EC2 recovery; NLB connection errors end.
The event ends in full (overall incident end time).
